entry: Tectonic belt of earthquakes and volcanoes surrounding most of the Pacific Ocean. It is about 40,000 km (25,000 mi) long and up to about 500 km (310 mi) wide. The belt contains between 750 and 915 active or dormant [[Volcano|volcanoes]], around two-thirds of the world total, and about 90% of the world's earthquakes, including most of its largest, occur within it. It was created by the subduction of several tectonic plates at convergent boundaries, forming [[Oceanic trench|oceanic trenches]], volcanic arcs and back-arc basins. More than 350 of its volcanoes have been active in historical times, and the four largest volcanic eruptions in the Holocene epoch all occurred there. Most of Earth's active volcanoes with summits above sea level lie within it, many of them [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcanoes]] such as [[Mount St. Helens]]. Its inclusion of areas such as the Antarctic Peninsula and western Indonesia is disputed.

Disk or torus of solid chunks of ice, rock and dust orbiting an astronomical object. Ring systems are also called planetary rings, and giant ring systems such as Saturn's may contain moonlets. All four giant planets, [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]], [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]], have ring systems, but Saturn's is the largest and most visible. Rings have also been detected around minor planets through occultations. Thicker planetary rings have been proposed to form from material inside the [[Roche limit]], from debris of a moon disrupted by a large impact, or from a moon torn apart by tidal stresses. Fainter rings can form when meteoroids strike moons. Some studies theorize that the Earth may have had a ring system during the mid-late [[Ordovician]] period. Phobos, a moon of Mars, is predicted to break up and form a ring in about 50 million years.

Branch of algebra concerned with rings, algebraic structures in which addition and multiplication have properties similar to those of the integers. Ring theory studies the structure of rings, their representations (or, equivalently, [[Module (mathematics)|modules]]), and special classes such as group rings and division rings. [[Commutative ring|Commutative rings]] are much better understood than noncommutative ones. [[Algebraic geometry]] and [[Algebraic number theory]] supply many examples of commutative rings and have driven the development of [[Commutative algebra]], a major area of modern mathematics. Many results belong to all three fields: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz is fundamental to algebraic geometry, while [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] is stated in elementary arithmetic but proved with both algebraic number theory and algebraic geometry. Since the 1980s, noncommutative geometry and quantum groups have led to a better understanding of noncommutative rings, especially noncommutative Noetherian rings.

English drummer, singer, songwriter and actor, best known as a member of the [[The Beatles|Beatles]]. He sang lead vocals on some Beatles recordings, including "Yellow Submarine". His playing emphasized feel over technical virtuosity. After the Beatles disbanded he had hits including the US top-ten "It Don't Come Easy", and his 1973 album *Ringo* was a top-ten release in both the UK and the US. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] twice, as a Beatle in 1988 and as a solo artist in 2015, and was appointed a Knight Bachelor in 2018 for services to music.

Ring system around Saturn, the most extensive of any planet in the Solar System. It is made almost entirely of water ice with a trace of rocky material. [[Galileo Galilei]] first observed the rings in 1610 without recognizing them, and in 1655 [[Christiaan Huygens]] described them as a disk. Many gaps are cleared by embedded moons or lie at destabilizing resonances with [[Moons of Saturn]], while others remain unexplained. There is no consensus on when the rings formed: models suggested an early origin, but newer Cassini data indicate a more recent one.

River of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, forming part of their border. It rises in south-central [[Colorado]] and flows 1,896 miles (3,051 km) to the [[Gulf of Mexico]], making it the fourth-longest river in the United States and North America by main stem. Its drainage basin covers 182,200 square miles (472,000 km2), or 336,000 square miles (870,000 km2) including adjacent endorheic basins. After crossing [[New Mexico]], it forms the border between [[Texas]] and the Mexican states of Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas. In Mexico it is called the Río Bravo (del Norte). Since the mid-twentieth century only 20 percent of its water has reached the Gulf, because of irrigation and urban use. A 260-mile (418 km) stretch in New Mexico and Texas is designated the Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River.

State in southern Brazil, bordered by [[Argentina]] and [[Uruguay]]. It is the fifth-most populous Brazilian state and the ninth-largest by area, with 497 municipalities. It has 5.4% of Brazil's population and produces 6.6% of its GDP. The capital and largest city is [[Porto Alegre]]. Before European arrival the region was inhabited mostly by the Guarani and Kaingang peoples. The first Europeans were [[Jesuits]], followed by settlers from the [[Azores]]. Conflicts of the 19th century included the Ragamuffin War and the [[Paraguayan War]], and large German and Italian migrations shaped the state.

Largest blackwater river in the world and the largest left tributary of the [[Amazon River]]. Known as the Guainía River in its upper course, it rises in Colombia and flows southeast through Colombia, Venezuela and Brazil. It carries about 14% of the water in the Amazon basin and is one of the world's ten largest rivers by average discharge, yet its sediment load is low: 5.76 million tonnes per year on average at [[Manaus]]. The Casiquiare canal links it with the [[Orinoco]], a unique connection between the Orinoco and Amazon basins. During the [[Wet season|wet season]], from April until October, the river floods the surrounding country for long distances. Near Manaus it meets the Solimões River to form the Amazon, in a phenomenon called the Meeting of Waters.

Second-largest city in Brazil (pop., 2025: 6 million), capital of [[Rio de Janeiro (state)|Rio de Janeiro state]]. Founded in 1565 as the seat of a Portuguese captaincy, it became the capital of the State of Brazil in 1763. When the Portuguese court arrived in 1808 it became the seat of the monarchy, and it remained the capital of the Empire and then the republic until 1960, when the capital moved to [[Brasília]]. It is one of the most visited cities in the Southern Hemisphere, known for [[Samba|samba]], [[Bossa nova|bossa nova]], Carnival and beaches such as Copacabana and Ipanema. Its landmarks include the statue of [[Christ the Redeemer (statue)|Christ the Redeemer]] on Corcovado mountain. Rio hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics, the first South American and Portuguese-speaking city to do so.

State in southeastern Brazil, with its capital in the city of [[Rio de Janeiro]]. It has the second-largest economy in Brazil, after [[São Paulo (state)|São Paulo]], and holds 8.2% of the national population while producing 9.2% of its GDP. It is the smallest state by area in the Southeast region but the third most populous, with over 16 million people at the 2022 census, making it the most densely populated state in Brazil. Its official demonym, fluminense, was sanctioned in 1783.

Form of civil disorder in which people commit public violence against authority figures and property. Riots typically destroy property, and targets include shops, cars, restaurants, state-owned institutions and religious buildings, though government offices are seldom targeted because of their protection. Riots often arise from poverty, unemployment, poor living conditions, governmental oppression, [[Tax|taxation]] or [[Conscription|conscription]], or conflict between [[Ethnicity|ethnic groups]] or religions, as in a [[Pogrom|pogrom]]. Sports riots may follow the outcome of a match or championship. Food riots may follow [[Harvest|harvest]] failures, hoarding or attacks by [[Locust|locusts]]. [[Police]] forces often struggle to control riots, using tear gas, CS gas and less-than-lethal weapons such as rubber bullets. Evidence suggests that rioters follow inverted social norms rather than irrational herd behavior.

American actress and dancer, one of the top stars of Hollywood's Golden Age. She was the second favorite pin-up girl for GIs in [[World War II]], after Betty Grable, and the press nicknamed her "The Love Goddess". She is best known for *Gilda* (1946), in which she played a femme fatale opposite Glenn Ford. She made two films with [[Fred Astaire]] and starred in *Cover Girl* (1944) with [[Gene Kelly]]. She received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960. In 1980 she was diagnosed with early-onset [[Alzheimer's disease]]; her public disclosure helped increase research funding.

Puerto Rican actress, dancer and singer, one of the few performers to have won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony (EGOT), and the Triple Crown of Acting. Her breakout role was Anita in *West Side Story* (1961), which won her the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress and made her the first Hispanic woman to win an Academy Award. She won a Tony for Best Featured Actress in a Play for *The Ritz* (1975). She also received Primetime Emmy Awards in consecutive years for *The Muppet Show* and *The Rockford Files*.

American rock and roll pioneer and a forefather of the Chicano rock movement. He is best known for "La Bamba", a rock adaptation of a Mexican folk song that became a hit in 1958, and for "Donna", which reached number two on the US chart. Valens was 17 when he died in a plane crash in Iowa that also killed [[Buddy Holly]] and J. P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. The crash became known as "The Day the Music Died". He was posthumously inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] and has a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

River in southern England, flowing through [[London]] to the North Sea. At 215 miles (346 km), it is the longest river entirely in England and the second-longest in the United Kingdom, after the River Severn. It rises at Thames Head in Gloucestershire and flows through Oxford, Reading and Windsor. Its tidal lower reaches, the Tideway, extend up to Teddington Lock. The river drops 55 metres (180 ft) from Oxford to the estuary and has 45 navigation locks. Its discharge is low for its length, as the Severn has an average discharge almost twice as large.

Typically triangular landform formed where a river deposits its sediment as it enters a sea, lake, reservoir or estuary. The name comes from the shape of the [[Nile]] Delta, which approximates the triangular Greek letter delta (Δ). As a river expands into standing water it slows, and sediment settles out to build the delta. Over time a channel builds a deltaic lobe, such as the bird's-foot of the [[Mississippi River|Mississippi]], and the river may breach its natural [[Levee|levees]] to take a shorter, steeper course. Deltas are major agricultural and population centers, can provide coastal defence, and are important carbon sinks on geologic timescales. Many face threats from [[Dam|dams]] that reduce sediment supply, land subsidence and sea-level rise.

Watercraft designed for inland navigation on lakes, rivers and artificial waterways. Riverboats are generally built as work boats for freight or passengers, or as luxury tour craft, and include dredgers, survey boats and fireboats. Because they do not have to withstand high winds or large waves, they are usually less sturdy than ocean vessels and can be built from light composite materials. Their size is limited by river width, depth and bridge height, and early paddle steamers on the [[Mississippi River]] could operate in water under two metres deep. A [[Ferry|ferry]] crosses a river, while a riverboat travels along it carrying passengers or cargo for revenue. The most famous riverboats operated on the [[Ohio River]] and [[Missouri River]]. Modern riverboats are usually screw-driven and powered by pairs of [[Diesel engine|diesel engines]].

Semi-permanent mechanical fastener with a head on one end. Installation flattens the tail of the shaft, called the shop head or buck-tail, into a shape like the head, creating a second head. Because of these two heads a rivet supports tension loads, but it is much more capable of supporting shear loads. Solid rivets are among the oldest and most reliable fasteners, found at [[Bronze Age]] sites, and [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]] spearheads from the Naqada culture, dated between 4400 and 3000 BC, have rivet holes. High-strength bolts have largely replaced structural [[Steel]] rivets, partly because skilled workers are costly; riveting once required four skilled workers. Rivets may be hammered by hand, driven with pneumatic hammers, or squeezed with machines.

Capital and largest city of [[Saudi Arabia]], on the Najd plateau of the central [[Arabian Peninsula]]. Riyadh has been a Saudi capital since the early 19th century. Ibn Saud regained the city in 1902, and in 1932 he named his kingdom Saudi Arabia with Riyadh as its capital. The city hosts the Consultative Assembly, the Council of Ministers and the king, and 23 of the 24 Saudi ministries are based there. It has 114 foreign embassies, most in the Diplomatic Quarter. Its population was 7 million in 2022. Over 500 foreign companies have moved regional bases there, including [[Lenovo]], [[Samsung]] and [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]].

Cycle sport discipline held primarily on paved roads. Road racing is the most popular professional form of bicycle racing in terms of competitors, events and spectators. The two most common formats are mass-start races, in which riders race to a set finish, and time trials, in which riders race a course alone against the clock. Stage races, or "tours", take several days. Professional racing originated in western Europe, centred in France, Spain, Italy and the Low Countries. The [[Tour de France]], first held in 1903, is the sport's biggest event and can attract over 500,000 roadside spectators a day. Cycling has been part of the [[Summer Olympic Games|Olympic Games]] since the modern sequence began in [[Athens]] in 1896.

Movement of people and goods on roads by bicycle, automobile, bus, truck, or by animals such as horses or oxen. Transport is commonly divided into goods and passengers, and licensing and safety rules often separate the two industries. Vans or pickup trucks serve short distances and light loads, while trucks suit larger shipments. Standard road networks were adopted by the [[Roman Empire|Romans]], Persians and other early empires. The Romans built solid roads with deep beds of crushed stone to keep them dry, and the [[Caliphate|Islamic Caliphate]] built tar-paved roads in [[Baghdad]]. Modern roads have defined lanes and signage, and the [[Interstate Highway System]] boosted commerce in the United States after World War II.

Genus of two species of fast-running ground cuckoos with long tails and crests. Roadrunners, also called chaparral birds, live in the southwestern and south-central [[United States]], Mexico and [[Central America]], usually in deserts. They can run at up to 32 km/h (20 mph) and generally prefer running to flying, though they fly to escape predators. They are opportunistic omnivores, eating insects, [[Lizard|lizards]], [[Rattlesnake|rattlesnakes]], rodents, spiders, scorpions, [[Cactus|cactus]] fruit and seeds. They are one of the few animals that prey on rattlesnakes, and the only real predator of [[Tarantula hawk|tarantula hawk wasps]].

Norwegian polar explorer and key figure of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration. From 1903 to 1906 he led the first expedition to traverse the [[Northwest Passage]], in the small sloop *Gjøa*. He then led the first party to reach the [[South Pole]], on December 14, 1911, after establishing a base at the Bay of Whales. In 1926 he and 15 other men flew in the airship *Norge* and became the first explorers verified to have reached the [[North Pole]]. Amundsen disappeared while flying on a rescue mission for the airship *Italia* in the [[Arctic]], and his remains were never found.

British author of children's literature and short stories, and a wartime fighter ace. Dahl was named after [[Roald Amundsen]] and was born to Norwegian parents in Wales. His children's books, among them *James and the Giant Peach*, *Charlie and the Chocolate Factory*, *Matilda* and *The BFG*, have an unsentimental, macabre and darkly comic mood, and often feature villainous adult enemies of their child characters. His short stories are known for unexpected endings. He served in the Royal Air Force in the Second World War as a fighter pilot and later as an intelligence officer. His books have sold more than 300 million copies worldwide.

Pair of English attempts to found a settlement on Roanoke Island, in present-day [[North Carolina]]. The first colony, a military outpost led by Ralph Lane, was established in 1585 and abandoned in 1586. A second group under John White arrived in 1587, and White's infant granddaughter Virginia Dare was born there. White went back to England for supplies, but the Anglo-Spanish War delayed his return until 1590. He found the settlement abandoned, with the word "CROATOAN" carved into the palisade. The colonists' fate remains unresolved, and the group became known as the "Lost Colony".
